title: What to report to keep a project on track
blurb: Know the factors a project typically reports on (time, cost, scope, quality, risks, benefits and more) and how reporting helps ensure success.
question: A railway signalling project's monthly report tells the board '75% complete, all green'. Two months later the project announces a four-month delay. What factors should a good progress report have covered to help ensure a successful outcome?

teach.body: Progress reporting tells decision-makers how the project is performing against its baseline and what is forecast, so they can act while there is still time. Factors typically reported: time, cost, scope, quality, risks and issues, the benefits forecast, resources, changes, stakeholder matters, dependencies, overall health (often a RAG status), the forecast to completion and decisions needed. In plain English: where are we, where are we heading, what is worrying us, and what do we need from you?

head: Factor
What is reported
rows: Spend vs budget; forecast at completion
Is the benefits forecast still on track?
Links to other projects and BAU

teach.h: A RAG dashboard over three months
teach.caption: The trend matters as much as the colour: Time has slid from green to red in two months. Definitions vary, but typically green = on track, amber = problems being managed, red = action or escalation needed.

teach.body: A useful report does three things. It looks back: actual progress against the baseline, with each variance explained (what happened, why, and the impact). It looks forward: the forecast to completion for time, cost and benefits, and the risks ahead. And it asks: which decisions or escalations are needed, and by when. A report that only lists completed tasks looks busy but gives the board nothing to act on.

steps.label: Compare
steps.sub: against the baseline in the PMP

teach.text: The '% complete, all green' trap: averaged progress can hide a slip on the critical path, and a report that is green on the outside but red inside (sometimes called a 'watermelon' report) delays decisions until it is too late. Flagging a variance without its impact, or listing activities without mentioning risks, are classic examples of ineffective reporting.

teach.h: Tailor the report to the audience
Reporting in linear and iterative life cycles

teach.body: Eastline's monthly report said '75% complete, all green', a figure based on spend. Underneath, the safety approval for the new software, on the critical path, was six weeks late; a supplier dependency had slipped; and the risk of losing a booked track closure had not been raised. A good report would have shown the critical-path slip, the forecast completion date, the risk, and one decision: approve a back-up track closure now. Two months later, it was too late.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Name the factor and say what is reported about it, e.g. 'Cost: actual spend against budget and the forecast at completion.'
Choose distinct factors (time, cost, quality, risks and issues, benefits) rather than five aspects of time.
Say why it helps ensure success: decision-makers can act early.
Show the look-forward element: forecasts and decisions needed, not just history.
Mention tailoring if the question involves different stakeholders.
Report against the baseline: time, cost, scope, quality.
Also report risks and issues, changes, dependencies, resources, stakeholders and the benefits forecast.
Give overall health (often RAG), the forecast to completion and the decisions needed.
Explain each variance's impact; averaged '% complete' can hide critical-path slips.
Tailor content to each audience. Iterative reports focus on scope delivered within fixed time and cost.

summary: You can now name the factors a project typically reports on (time, cost, scope, quality, risks and issues, benefits, resources, changes, stakeholders, dependencies, overall status, forecast and decisions needed). You can also explain why honest, forward-looking, tailored reporting helps ensure a successful outcome.

A.q: Which set of factors would a project progress report to the sponsor typically cover?
options: Market share, profit margin and share price
Each team member's appraisal and sickness
Supplier tender scores and bid prices only
Time, cost, quality, risks and issues
A.why: Progress reports cover performance against the baseline (time, cost, scope, quality), risks and issues, plus benefits, resources, changes and the decisions needed.

whyNot.0: These are organisational financial measures, not project progress factors.
whyNot.1: Individual HR matters belong to line management, not a project progress report.
whyNot.2: Tender scores are a procurement record, not a measure of project progress.

A.q: Why should a progress report include a forecast to completion as well as progress to date?
options: So that the team's past performance can be graded
So decision-makers can act before problems land
Because the baseline is no longer needed
Because forecasts replace the risk register
A.why: Forecasts show where the project is heading, so the sponsor and board can take action or decisions while there is still time to change the outcome.

whyNot.0: Reporting is about steering the project, not grading the team.
whyNot.2: Forecasts are compared with the baseline, so it is still needed.
whyNot.3: Risks are still managed in the register; forecasts and risks are reported side by side.

A.q: In a typical RAG status report, what does amber usually signal?
options: Problems exist but are being managed
The project has been closed down early
All work has been formally accepted
Every tolerance has been exceeded
A.why: Definitions vary by organisation, but amber typically means at risk: problems exist but are being managed within tolerance. Red usually means action or escalation is needed.

whyNot.1: Closure is not a RAG status; it would be reported as a decision or milestone.
whyNot.2: Formal acceptance would be reported as a completed milestone, not as amber.
whyNot.3: Exceeding tolerances would normally be shown as red and escalated.

B.q: A rail project's monthly report says '75% complete, all green', yet a safety approval on the critical path is six weeks late. What is the main flaw in this reporting?
options: It was issued far too often to stay accurate
It should have gone only to the team
Averaged progress hid a critical-path slip
It used RAG colours instead of numbers
B.why: An overall percentage can look healthy while a critical-path activity is late. Good reports highlight critical slips, their impact and the forecast end date.

whyNot.0: Monthly reporting is a normal frequency; the problem is the content, not how often it was issued.
whyNot.1: The board needed this information most, as they had decisions to take.
whyNot.3: RAG colours are fine if they are honest; here they did not reflect reality.

B.q: Which of these is LEAST useful in a progress report to a project board?
options: A list of every task completed
Variance against the baseline
Decisions the board must take
Key risks and how they are trending
B.why: A task list shows activity, not performance. A board needs variances, forecasts, risks and the decisions it must make.

whyNot.1: Variance against the baseline is central: it shows whether the project is on track.
whyNot.2: Decisions needed are exactly what a board report should ask for.
whyNot.3: Key risks and their trend help the board anticipate problems.

B.q: A project manager sends the same 30-page report to the board and to site supervisors every week. What is the main risk?
options: The report will breach data protection law
The board will approve every change request
Supervisors will take over the sponsor's role
Neither group gets what it needs to act on
B.why: Different audiences need different detail: the board needs summary, forecast and decisions; supervisors need specific tasks and dates. One format fits neither.

whyNot.0: A long report is not in itself a data protection breach.
whyNot.1: Report length does not cause the board to approve changes.
whyNot.2: Receiving a report does not change anyone's governance role.

C.q: An iterative team works in fixed four-week time boxes with a fixed budget. What would its progress reports focus on most?
options: Cost overruns in each time box
Scope delivered against priorities
Changes to the fixed end date
Variance against a fixed full scope
C.why: With time and cost fixed, scope is the variable, so reports focus on which prioritised features (Must haves first) have been delivered, often using burn-down charts and demos.

whyNot.0: Cost is fixed per time box, so overruns should not be the main focus.
whyNot.2: Time boxes do not move; the end date is fixed.
whyNot.3: Iterative projects do not baseline the full detailed scope up front.

C.q: A report flags a £50k overspend on testing but says nothing more about it. What is the most important missing element?
options: The names of the testers involved
A full list of every test carried out
Its impact on forecast and objectives
A recommendation to cut all testing
C.why: Variances need explaining: the cause, the impact on forecast cost, time and objectives, and the action proposed.

whyNot.0: Naming individuals does not help decision-makers understand the impact.
whyNot.1: A test list adds detail but not the impact the board needs.
whyNot.3: Cutting all testing would threaten quality; a recommendation must follow from impact analysis.

C.q: Which THREE should a monthly report to a sponsor include? (1) risks and issues needing escalation (2) decisions the sponsor must take (3) the forecast to completion (4) copies of every email sent that month
options: 1, 2 and 3
1, 2 and 4
1, 3 and 4
2, 3 and 4
C.why: Escalations, decisions needed and forecasts are what a sponsor needs to steer the project. Email copies are raw data, not reporting.

whyNot.1: Item 4 is wrong: copying every email buries the important messages.
whyNot.2: Item 4 is wrong, and item 2 (decisions needed) is missing.
whyNot.3: Item 4 is wrong, and item 1 (risks and issues needing escalation) is missing.

reteach.title: Think of a kitchen refit
reteach.question: Three weeks into your kitchen refit, one builder says 'nearly there, all fine'. Another sends a short written update. What makes the second one useful?

blocks.body: 'Nearly there, all fine' feels reassuring until the fitter disappears for a week. A useful update says: units fitted, worktops a week late because of the supplier; £300 over budget because a rotten joist was found; a risk that the tiles you chose are being discontinued; and one decision: pick replacement tiles by Friday or the finish slips again. It covers time, cost, quality, risks and what you need to decide.

blocks.text: 'Nearly there' is the kitchen version of '75% complete, all green'. Without a forecast, the risks and the decisions needed, you cannot act until it is too late.

explain.body: Time, cost, scope and quality are measured against the baselines in the approved PMP: milestones hit or missed, spend against budget and forecast, changes approved, and test or acceptance results.

test.q: Which pair of factors shows a sponsor whether a project is on schedule and on budget?
options: Benefits and stakeholder views
Risks and external dependencies
Quality and resource levels
Time and cost against baseline
test.why: Schedule and budget performance are shown by reporting time and cost against the approved baseline.

whyNot.0: Benefits and stakeholder views matter, but they do not show schedule or budget position.
whyNot.1: Risks and dependencies affect the future, but they do not measure current schedule and cost.
whyNot.2: Quality and resources are separate factors from schedule and budget.

explain.body: Reports show the top risks and how they are trending, open issues and any needing escalation, changes requested and approved, and dependencies on other projects or BAU. These are the early warnings.

test.q: Why should new risks appear in a status report even when every task is on schedule?
options: So the team can be held to blame later
So they can be acted on before they hit
Because risks must be closed each month
Because the PMO counts them for budgets
test.why: Reporting emerging risks early gives time to plan and take responses before they turn into issues.

whyNot.0: Reporting exists to support decisions, not to assign blame.
whyNot.2: Risks are closed when they pass or occur, not on a monthly cycle.
whyNot.3: Risk reporting is about managing uncertainty, not PMO budgeting.

explain.body: The benefits forecast shows whether the business case still holds. Resource reporting flags shortfalls before they cause delays. Stakeholder matters show where support or concern is shifting.

explain.caption: A resource gap reported in advance can be fixed; one discovered on the day becomes a delay.

test.q: Why report the benefits forecast during delivery, not only after handover?
options: Because benefits are paid out each month
Because the PM personally owns each benefit
So the case can be re-tested in time to act
So that benefits reviews are not needed
test.why: If forecast benefits fall, the sponsor can re-test the business case and re-plan or stop while action still makes a difference.

whyNot.0: Benefits are improvements, not monthly payments.
whyNot.1: The sponsor is accountable for benefits, not the PM.
whyNot.3: Benefits reviews are still needed, especially after handover.

explain.body: Every report should end with the overall status, where the project is heading and what is needed from its readers. Tailor the detail: summary and exceptions for the board, specifics for the team.

test.q: What should every progress report to a project board make clear?
options: The decisions and support needed
A list of the team's holiday dates
The full text of the project plan
A summary of last month's report
test.why: Reports exist to support decisions, so they should state clearly what the board needs to decide or provide.

whyNot.1: Holiday dates are detail for resource planning, not a board report.
whyNot.2: The PMP is the baseline; reports compare against it rather than repeating it.
whyNot.3: Repeating last month adds nothing; the board needs current status and forecast.
